advances: Ordinary planar triangles with a balanced three-cap circuit. This characterizes equality without a cap-fraction ceiling or a restriction to centroid cuts.

proof:
Apply the all-incidence triangle cubic theorem [b649b1adca5662b7](../facts/b649b1adca5662b7.md) with exactly the above ordinary areas and coarea lengths. It gives the inequality, strictness for two strictly captured vertices, and weak distinct-vertex incidence at equality. In that incidence write $h_i=v_i\cdot(P_i-y)>0$. The intercept on edge $P_iP_j$ is at fraction $h_i/L_{ij}\in(0,1]$ from $P_i$. Thus the cap is a triangle of area $Q_i=kh_i^2/(L_{ij}L_{i\ell})=h_i\sigma_i/2$. These formulas hold also when an intercept is at $P_j$. Both intercepts cannot equal one, since the cutting line contains the interior point $y$. Consequently $M=H/2$ and the asserted formula for $f_i^2$ follows. Balance of the normals makes $H=\sum_i v_i\cdot P_i$ independent of $y$.

For the normalized edge-fraction matrix of the all-incidence theorem, let $R_{ij}$ be the captured fraction of the edge opposite $P_j$. In this labeling $R_{ii}=0$ and $R_{ij}=h_i/L_{i\ell}$ for $j\ne i$ and remaining index $\ell$. Its normalized entries are $X_{ij}=kR_{ij}/(\sigma_iM)$, so $X_{ij}=L_{ij}/H$ off the diagonal. This identifies the two stochastic cycle products, including at the knots, with the two drop products divided by $H^3$. Therefore equality in the theorem is exactly their equality. Choosing $\mu_1>0$ and setting $\mu_2=\mu_1L_{12}/L_{21}$ and $\mu_3=\mu_1L_{13}/L_{31}$ gives detailed balance on every pair exactly when the cycle products agree. The same equations show uniqueness up to scale.

Assume detailed balance. Define a linear map $A$ by $A(P_i-P_j)=\mu_i v_i-\mu_jv_j$ on two independent edge differences. These equations also hold on the third difference by addition. Symmetry follows by testing on $P_1-P_2,P_1-P_3$: the difference between the two mixed products is
$$
\mu_1(L_{12}-L_{13})-\mu_3(L_{32}-L_{31})+\mu_2(L_{23}-L_{21})=0.
$$
Write $\lambda_i=1/\mu_i$, $\Lambda=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and $x_i=P_i-O$. Then $\sum_i\lambda_i x_i=0$ and averaging the edge-map formulas using $\sum_i v_i=0$ gives $Ax_i=\mu_i v_i$. The quadratic form $q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ has a common value $R$ on the $x_i$, since $q(x_i)-q(x_j)=\mu_iL_{ij}-\mu_jL_{ji}$. Moreover $q(P_i-P_j)=2\mu_iL_{ij}>0$. By expanding the quadratic form using $\sum_i\lambda_i x_i=0$,
$$
\Lambda^2R=\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i\lambda_jq(P_i-P_j)>0.
$$

For $i\ne j$ put $G_{ij}=x_i^{\mathsf T}Ax_j$. The edge identity gives $G_{ij}=R-\mu_iL_{ij}<R$. Taking the quadratic form of $\lambda_i x_i+\lambda_jx_j=-\lambda_\ell x_\ell$ gives $G_{ij}/R=(\lambda_\ell^2-\lambda_i^2-\lambda_j^2)/(2\lambda_i\lambda_j)$. Thus the three inequalities $G_{ij}<R$ imply the three strict triangle inequalities on the $\lambda_i$. They imply $\lambda_\ell>|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|$ and hence $G_{ij}>-R$. Since $O$ is strictly interior, any two of the $x_i$ are independent. On such a basis the quadratic form has diagonal entries $R>0$ and determinant $R^2-G_{ij}^2>0$. Thus $A$ is positive definite.

The ellipse $q(x-O)\le R$ has the desired outward normals since $Ax_i=\mu_i v_i$. Conversely, if an ellipse with positive definite form $A$ and center $O$ has these outward normals, write $A(P_i-O)=\mu_i v_i$ with $\mu_i>0$. The equal values of its quadratic form at $P_i,P_j$ give detailed balance on that pair by subtraction. The edge-map construction then determines $A$ up to the common scale of the weights, and the same weighted averaging identifies $O$.

§4, arbitrary cut incidence and vertex-on-cut equality

statement:
Let $T$ be a nondegenerate planar triangle with interior source $y$ and nonzero spanning normals $v_i$ summing to zero. Put $k=|T|$, $Q_i=|T\cap\{v_i\cdot(x-y)\ge0\}|$, $\sigma_i=\mathcal H^1(T\cap\{v_i\cdot(x-y)=0\})/\lVert v_i\rVert$, $M=\sum_iQ_i/\sigma_i$, and $f_i=2\sqrt{kQ_i}/(\sigma_iM)$. Then $\sum_i f_i^2+\prod_i f_i\le4$, strictly if any cap strictly captures two vertices. Equality holds precisely when the vertices can be labeled $P_i$ so that $v_i\cdot(P_i-y)>0$ and $v_i\cdot(P_j-y)\le0$ for $j\ne i$, and an ellipse through the three $P_i$ has outward normals at them that are positive multiples of $v_i$.

In this weak incidence regime put $L_{ij}=v_i\cdot(P_i-P_j)>0$ and $H=\sum_i v_i\cdot(P_i-y)$. Then $f_i^2=4L_{ij}L_{i\ell}/H^2$ for $\{i,j,\ell\}=\{1,2,3\}$ and the row vector is independent of $y$ within the same labeled incidence regime. The ellipse condition is equivalent to $L_{12}L_{23}L_{31}=L_{13}L_{32}L_{21}$ and to the existence of $\mu_i>0$ with $\mu_iL_{ij}=\mu_jL_{ji}$. These weights are unique up to scale. The ellipse center is $O=(\sum_iP_i/\mu_i)/(\sum_i1/\mu_i)$, strictly inside $T$, and its defining quadratic form is positive definite and determined up to positive scale.
title: Circumellipses characterize ordinary triangle cubic equality
